articleTitle: Geothermal energy: Significant resource of the future
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Geothermal energy is the heat of the earth's interior created by vast sources of energy from the hot magma of the interior. Heat releases through radioactive decay of minerals, interior friction, etc. The most obvious surface indications are hot springs, geysers and fumeroles. With present technology the earth's heat can be used only through water in the form of steam and hot water under pressure. In four of the six presently known types of geothermal resources, nature provides us with both the heat and the water together. It is for this reason that I predict the early and large-scale development of these four types of geothermal resources whereas the other two types may require longer development periods.

articleTitle: Television frequency assignment plan for bands III, IV and V in the republic of South Africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The previously registered television frequency assignment plan for South Africa was found to be inadequate for the anticipated requirements. The Republic with its multilingual society posed problems which required a special approach. This paper outlines the method by which a new plan was developed and defines all the factors associated with the receiver, transmitter, propagation conditions and terrain. The new plan provides at least four channels to most stations and seven to stations in the major urban areas. A subsidiary plan was derived in order to provide transmitter frequencies for gaps which would occur in the national coverage.

articleTitle: Lightning phenomena in the aerospace environment
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: At least four and perhaps five basic modes of lightning discharge in thunderstorms are identified, viz, positive or negative discharges to the earth, short intracloud or long horizontal intercloud discharges and possibly discharges to the upper atmosphere. The latter are predicted by a cylindrical model of the cloud which helps to explain why under given circumstances one type of discharge should occur rather than another. A new model of the mechanism of the negative discharge to earth is proposed. In this model it is assumed that a bipolar leader deposits negative charge in a cylindrical corona envelope and over-discharges during the return stroke to leave the channel positively charged. This process is followed by a further breakdown in the cloud area to provide the electrons for neutralising this ionic charge. The availability of mobile electrons is restricted, and the process may or may not continue. Subsequent strokes may, however, occur depending upon the maintenance or not of the breakdown fields within the cloud. By this mechanism, the positive discharge could continue owing to the availability of a copious supply of electrons from the earth, and will not stop until most charge is neutralised. Parameters of individual first and subsequent strokes of both positive and negative lightning flashes are given from an analysis of Berger's measurements on Mount San Salvatore and attention is drawn to some parameters which differ widely, the variations possibly being due to differences in lightning under various climatic conditions.

articleTitle: Microwave holography and the location of knife-edge obstacles on line of sight microwave routes
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The problem of determining the positions of (multiple) knife-edge obstacles on line-of-sight microwave routes directly from standard height-intensity measurements is treated theoretically. The analysis invokes holographic principles, the height-intensity distribution itself being regarded as a (microwave) hologram. The necessary processing is performed digitally, and is based on the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. It is demonstrated that edge location in two dimensions (range and height) is impractical. The ‘quality’ of the I-D (height only) image of a scattering edge is shown to be improved in the case of simultaneous scanning of source and receiver. The problem of noise is simulated and the effect of a finite-size receiving aperture is discussed.

abstract: The International Energy Agency (IEA) was established in November, 1974 and has 18 participants: Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Norway, Netherlands, West Germany, Japan, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, United Kingdom and United States. To avoid a recurrence of the unacceptable costs of the 1973-74 Arab oil embargo, these nations resolved to develop a capability to deal with future supply interruptions in a cooperative framework. Part of this program was a decision to create a $25 000 million safety net for mutual support in financial crisis. IEA countries undertook three additional inter-related commitments to build emergency oil reserves, to develop conservation programs and in an emergency to allocate available oil.

articleTitle: A computer model for the simulation and evaluation of line scanners
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: This paper describes the basic principles concerned in the design of an airborne line scanning system, together with a method of theoretically evaluating system performance. It also describes a computer software model that was constructed for the calculation of scanner performance parameters. This model was validated by comparing its predictions with the manufacturer specifications for a number of commercially available scanners. 6 Summary and conclusions The operation of a basic line scanner has been described and its performance characteristics derived from Planck's radiation law and electro-optical principles. A computer model was constructed to calculate performance parameters from component and system specifications. This model accurately predicts scanner performance in that calculated NETD's agree well with those provided by manufacturers.

articleTitle: Lightning phenomena in the aerospace environment
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Most jet aircraft cruise at an altitude above 10 km, which is usually higher than the clouds, and the planes are not then in danger of being struck by lightning. While climbing or descending, however, aircraft are liable to be struck by intra-cloud or cloud to ground lightning. Records of lightning damage kept by the South African Airways and extending over a period of 26 years show that from about 1956 the occurrence of lightning strikes decreased from a peak of 3,5 down to 1,8 strikes per 10 000 flying hours. Only 14 per cent of the lightning strikes to modern high-flying aircraft occurred whilst the aircraft were cruising. Damage to the aircraft frame or instruments occurred in 40 per cent of the strikes reported. It was also shown that the majority of strikes to aircraft occurred below a height of 7 km, the mean altitude being between 3 and 5 km above sea level. The report concludes by suggesting that the time spent by aircraft below 7 km should be kept to a minimum, and that the degree of occurrence of lightning over airports should be ascertained.

articleTitle: South Africa's role in the development and use of radar in world war 2
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: I must ask you to forget that we are in the Seventies where the achievements of science arc taken for granted, and to think back to the late thirties when the Spanish Civil War made it clear to the British public that, in any major war in Europe, they would be in the front line. In the absence of any method of detecting and observing the movements of aircraft there appeared to be no real defence against the bomber by day, let alone by night. How then was the problem of airborne attack on Great Britain largely solved and, in the latter part of the War, a major bombing offensive against occupied Europe maintained? Radar certainly was not solely responsible for this achievement, but radar, or more strictly superiority in radar, played an altogether indispensable role in both defence and offence. Radar also played an indispensable role in antisubmarine warfare which was equally vital to Britain's survival.

articleTitle: Source impedance characteristics and their effect on surge arrester design
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The system parameters usually considered in the application of surge arresters on high voltage transmission lines have not included, for the most part, the magnitude or character of the source impedance. This omission is a carryover from older arrester designs which had an extremely high series resistance, limiting arrester current to a relatively low value, and literally swamping any effect on arrester current from either power frequency or line surge impedance. As transmission voltages have steadily increased in the last two decades, arrester protective levels had to decrease, and this resulted in greatly reduced arrester impedances. This is evidenced by the high follow current magnitude of modern H V and E H V arresters which, in some designs, has reached 1 000 amperes at rated voltage. Although surge arresters have been applied for many years on circuits of low source impedance, the problems encountered on these circuits have not generally been of sufficient magnitude to influence arrester construction or design. Further, design or type tests in arrester standards are not aimed at exploring performance under these unusual system conditions. Special laboratory tests designed for this purpose can determine durability limits of conventional arrester development of designs and aid in evaluation and application information. The most important parameter to be observed in such tests is the initial current through the arrester and its relation magnitude and duration to the specific arrester capability.

articleTitle: Krisisse en uitdagings in kragvoorsiening: Crises and challenges in energy supply
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: During the last few years three so called crises which affect today's energy supply situation have made an appearance. These are: (a) The environmental crisis (b) The energy crisis (c) The economic and financial crisis. The first of these is the easiest to solve and its effect is in any case today being masked by the other two. The more important problems which have followed these crises are discussed. It has become clear that the excessive use of oil as a fuel — because it was until recently very cheap by any standards — has been the factor which plunged the world into the energy crisis — more particularly into an oil crisis. This has had severe economic consequences, the end of which is not yet in sight. It is mainly in the field of fuel for the propulsion of private and public transport vehicles that the new higher cost of oil and its potential shortage has given rise to problems. The whole spectrum of available energy sources is reviewed, and it is shown that the application of known engineering principles plus of course further research and development will make it possible to utilise one or more of the existing alternative energy sources to replace oil in any of its present applications including as a fuel for the internal combustion engine. It is also pointed out that much of the world's energy consumption at present is either unnecessary or unduly wasteful. Savings in energy consumption are possible in all sorts of ways through the application of existing engineering principles. Certain areas are shown to exist where intensive research effort has produced great savings in energy consumption as well as progress in other ways. A plea is made for similar efforts in other directions where equally large possibilities for energy conservation and saving exist.
